title: Composition versus inheritance
objective: Build objects from parts they have (composition) instead of deep is-a trees, so features combine without a class for every mix.

sources.title: Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (Addison-Wesley, 1994), chapter 1: "Favor object composition over class inheritance"
Joshua Bloch, Effective Java, 3rd edition (Addison-Wesley, 2018): "Favor composition over inheritance"

simplifies: Inheritance isn't bad: it fits when a subclass truly is a kind of its parent and can stand in for it everywhere (next lesson: Liskov). The rule of thumb is to prefer composition, not to ban inheritance.

steps.caption: Notifications start with a base class, and subclasses for email and SMS. So far, so good.
Then urgent messages (sent at once, with a sound): UrgentEmail and UrgentSms. Each option doubles the classes.

predict.prompt: Push notifications arrive next. How many new classes does this tree need?

options.explanation: Right. Every channel needs every option: channels × options classes.
Urgent push would still need its own subclass.
There's no class that sends push notifications yet.

steps.caption: Inheriting just to reuse code also leaks. A Stack that inherits from list gets insert() and sort() too.

predict.prompt: What does s.insert(0, 'oops') do to the stack?

options.text: It puts an item at the bottom, breaking last in, first out
options.explanation: Right. Stack inherited every list method, including ones that break its own rule.
insert() is inherited from list, so it works.
It changes the list underneath the stack.

steps.caption: Composition: a Notification has a Channel (how to deliver) and a Delivery policy (when). Each is a small interface.
Mixing is now just picking parts: any channel with any policy, no subclass per mix.
Adding push notifications is one new Channel class. Three channels and two policies give six behaviours from small parts.

predict.prompt: With composition, adding push notifications means…

options.text: One new class that implements Channel
options.explanation: Right. It works with every Delivery policy straight away.
No subclass per mix any more.
Notification only knows the Channel interface, so it doesn't change.

exercise.change: Every message must be retried if sending fails.
exercise.hint: Each subclass overrides send() completely. Where does sending actually happen?

options.text: Give Notification a Channel and a Delivery (composition), and put the retry in its one send()
options.explanation: Right. Sending happens in one place, so the retry is written once.

options.text: Add a RetryingNote subclass under each class
options.explanation: That doubles the tree again, and the next feature doubles it once more.

options.text: Copy the retry loop into a helper and call it from each send()
options.explanation: Less copying, but all four classes still change, and the next feature repeats that.

exercise.explain: Notification.send() is the one place a message goes out (it calls channel.deliver), so the retry is one edit. The tree needed the same change in every subclass, because each overrode send().

options.text: When the subclass truly is a kind of the parent and works anywhere the parent does
options.explanation: Right. That's a real is-a relationship, not just shared code.

options.text: Whenever two classes share some code
options.explanation: That's reuse; composition shares code without tying the classes together.
The advice is to prefer composition, not to ban inheritance.

quiz.prompt: Why does class Stack(list) cause trouble?

options.text: Stack inherits insert(), sort() and more, so callers can break last in, first out
options.explanation: Right. Composition (a Stack that has a list) exposes only push() and pop().
Python allows it; the design is the problem.
